common_name: Tidal Wave Silver Petunia (Upright Vigorous Lavender-Silver Spreading Petunia)

planting.note: Plant transplants after all frost danger has passed in well-drained, fertile soil in full sun; Tidal Wave grows upright and mounding rather than trailing flat like the original Wave, so it can be massed as a hedge-like bedding display as well as a large container filler.

directions: Tidal Wave Silver was bred to grow taller and more upright than the ground-hugging original Wave series, forming a dense, self-branching mound that still spreads outward without sprawling flat. Its pale lilac-silver flowers with a soft yellow throat cover the plant continuously from spring through frost with strong heat tolerance and little need for deadheading. The larger, sturdier habit makes it useful as an informal summer hedge or mass planting where a bigger, bushier petunia is wanted. Fertilize regularly through the season to sustain its vigorous growth and heavy bloom.

common_name: Tidal Wave Cherry Petunia (Upright Vigorous Cherry-Red Spreading Petunia)

planting.note: Plant transplants after all frost danger has passed in well-drained, fertile soil in full sun; Tidal Wave's tall, self-branching mound holds up better in summer storms than trailing Wave types, making it a good choice for exposed beds.

directions: Tidal Wave Cherry carries the same tall, bushy, self-branching habit as the rest of the Tidal Wave line but in a saturated cherry-red that reads brighter and warmer than the deep magenta of the original Wave series. The upright growth needs no pinching to stay full and holds its shape through summer rain and wind better than lower-growing spreading petunias. It blooms heavily from spring to frost with good heat tolerance and largely self-cleans. Feed on a regular schedule to keep the vigorous, densely branched plants flowering at full strength.

common_name: Wave Carmine Velour Petunia (Velvety Deep Carmine-Red Spreading Petunia)

planting.note: Plant transplants after all frost danger has passed in well-drained, fertile soil in full sun; the low, ground-hugging spread suits it to slopes, retaining walls, and large hanging baskets alongside other Wave colors.

directions: Wave Carmine Velour brings a rich, velvety carmine-red to the original low-growing, ground-hugging Wave habit, with a deeper, warmer saturation than the classic Purple Wave and a subtle sheen that shows best in strong sunlight. It spreads fast and wide while staying low, making it useful as a flowering groundcover, slope cover, or spiller for large containers and window boxes. Bloom is continuous from spring through frost with minimal deadheading needed. Regular fertilizing keeps the vigorous, wide-spreading growth flowering strongly all season.

common_name: Easy Wave Blue Petunia (Compact Mounding Violet-Blue Spreading Petunia)

planting.note: Transplant after the last frost into containers, hanging baskets, or beds; the compact, self-branching mound needs less initial spacing than the original Wave series.

directions: Easy Wave Blue delivers a true violet-blue flower on the compact, self-branching mound that defines the Easy Wave line, needing no pinching to stay full and dense the way older wave-type petunias required. It spreads readily but stays more contained than the original Wave series, fitting hanging baskets and window boxes as easily as landscape beds. Blooms are largely self-cleaning, so only an occasional light trim is needed to refresh the plant midseason. Fertilize regularly with a bloom-boosting formula to keep the blue color vivid through summer heat.

common_name: Easy Wave White Petunia (Compact Mounding Pure White Spreading Petunia)

planting.note: Transplant after the last frost into containers, hanging baskets, or beds; the clean white flowers make this Easy Wave color a common anchor for mixed-color plantings.

directions: Easy Wave White covers its compact, self-branching mound in crisp, pure white blooms that brighten mixed plantings and show well even in low evening light. Like the rest of the Easy Wave series it needs no pinching to stay full and produces largely self-cleaning flowers, so deadheading demands are low. It spreads into a dense, weed-suppressing mat in beds or spills gracefully from hanging baskets and window boxes. Water and feed on a regular schedule through the heat of summer to keep the white color from fading and to sustain nonstop bloom to frost.

common_name: Shock Wave Coral Crush Petunia (Small-Flowered Coral-Pink Spreading Petunia)
scientific_name: Petunia x hybrida 'Shock Wave Coral Crush'

planting.note: Plant out once frost danger has passed; the small, prolific flowers and mounding-spreading habit suit both beds and mixed containers.

directions: Shock Wave Coral Crush covers its low, mounding-spreading habit in small, saturated coral-pink flowers produced in far greater numbers than a standard-flowered petunia, giving the plant a solid sheet of color from a distance. Its diminutive bloom size sheds water and bounces back from heavy summer rain faster than large-flowered petunias, keeping the display tidy without deadheading. Grow it in well-drained soil or potting mix under full sun for the heaviest flower count. Feed regularly with a diluted liquid fertilizer to sustain vigorous, continuous bloom through the hottest part of the season.

common_name: Shock Wave Deep Purple Petunia (Small-Flowered Rich Purple Spreading Petunia)
scientific_name: Petunia x hybrida 'Shock Wave Deep Purple'

planting.note: Set out transplants after the last frost; the small-flowered, mounding-spreading habit fills beds and mixed containers quickly.

directions: Shock Wave Deep Purple produces an especially heavy flush of small, rich purple flowers on the compact, self-cleaning, rain-tolerant habit that distinguishes the Shock Wave line from the larger-flowered original Wave series. Its numerous small blooms recover from summer downpours faster than big-flowered petunias, keeping the color solid without deadheading. Grow in well-drained soil or potting mix in full sun, watering consistently since containers and raised beds dry faster than in-ground plantings. Feed every two to three weeks with a balanced fertilizer to sustain the dense purple flower cover through summer.

common_name: Shock Wave Ivory Petunia (Small-Flowered Creamy Ivory Spreading Petunia)

planting.note: Set out transplants after the last frost; the soft ivory color blends easily with brighter Shock Wave shades in mixed containers and beds.

directions: Shock Wave Ivory softens the intense colors typical of the Shock Wave line with a warm, creamy ivory bloom that reads almost white in strong sun but shows a gentle buttery cast in cooler light. The small flowers are produced in exceptional numbers on a compact, self-cleaning, mounding-spreading habit that shrugs off summer rain better than large-flowered petunias. Grow in well-drained soil or potting mix in full sun, keeping moisture consistent through hot spells. Feed regularly with a diluted liquid fertilizer to keep the ivory flowers abundant and bright through the season.

common_name: Supertunia Vista Fuchsia Petunia (Vibrant Fuchsia-Pink Vigorous Spreading Petunia)

planting.note: Plant vegetatively propagated transplants after all frost danger has passed in fertile, well-drained soil; this vigorous fuchsia Vista selection needs the same generous spacing as its Bubblegum and Jazzberry series-mates.

directions: Supertunia Vista Fuchsia produces electric, hot-pink-purple flowers in the same outsized volume and vigor that defines the Vista series, mounding upward before trailing widely to fill large containers, hanging baskets, or landscape mass plantings. The intense fuchsia color holds up in full summer sun and stands out even at a distance, pairing well with silver- or chartreuse-foliage companions. It blooms continuously from spring to frost without deadheading. Regular fertilizing supports the exceptionally vigorous growth, and a midseason trim can rejuvenate the planting if it becomes leggy in peak summer heat.

common_name: Supertunia Mini Vista Pink Star Petunia (Compact Small-Flowered Pink-and-White Star Petunia)
scientific_name: Petunia x hybrida 'Mini Vista Pink Star'

planting.note: Plant vegetatively propagated transplants after all frost danger has passed in well-drained, fertile soil; Mini Vista's smaller, denser habit suits hanging baskets and smaller containers better than the full-sized Vista series.

directions: Supertunia Mini Vista Pink Star bears smaller, more numerous flowers than the standard Vista line, each bubblegum-pink bloom marked with a subtle pale-star pattern radiating from its throat. It grows in a tighter, more compact mound than Vista Bubblegum or Jazzberry, making it a better fit for smaller pots and mixed hanging baskets while still flowering heavily from spring to frost. Deadheading is unnecessary thanks to its self-cleaning habit. Feed regularly through the season to keep the abundant small blooms coming, and shear back lightly if growth becomes crowded in midsummer heat.

common_name: Supertunia Priscilla Petunia (Ruffled Pink-and-Cream Picotee Spreading Petunia)

planting.note: Plant vegetatively propagated transplants after all frost danger has passed in well-drained, fertile soil in full sun; Priscilla's ruffled petal edges show best when plants are not crowded, so allow full spacing.

directions: Supertunia Priscilla stands apart from the solid-colored Supertunia lineup with heavily ruffled, frilled petals in soft pink shading to a creamy-white picotee edge, giving each bloom a lacy, old-fashioned look. The mounding, moderately spreading habit fills containers and beds without the extreme vigor of the Vista series, making it easier to keep in scale in smaller plantings. It flowers continuously from spring through frost and needs little deadheading thanks to its self-cleaning blooms. Fertilize regularly and give it a light midsummer trim if the ruffled flowers start to look sparse in peak heat.

common_name: Crazytunia Black Mamba Petunia (Near-Black Deep Purple Star-Throated Petunia)

planting.note: Plant vegetatively propagated transplants after all frost danger has passed in well-drained, fertile soil in full sun; Black Mamba's near-black color deepens further in cooler weather and can bleach slightly under the most intense midsummer sun.

directions: Crazytunia Black Mamba is part of a novelty series bred for bold, unusual color patterns, offering an intensely dark, near-black bloom accented by a small red-and-yellow starburst deep in the throat. The compact, mounding-spreading habit fits containers and small beds where a striking accent color is wanted alongside brighter companion annuals. It flowers from spring to frost with minimal deadheading required thanks to its self-cleaning blooms. Grow in full sun for the darkest color saturation, and fertilize regularly to sustain vigorous, continuous bloom through the season.

common_name: Surfinia Sky Blue Petunia (Vigorous Trailing Pale Blue Petunia)

planting.note: Plant vegetatively propagated transplants after all frost danger has passed in well-drained, fertile soil in full sun; Surfinia's long trailing stems benefit from elevated hanging baskets or tall containers so the growth can cascade freely.

directions: Surfinia Sky Blue carries the original Suntory Surfinia line's trademark vigor and long, cascading trailing stems, here in a clear, pale sky-blue that lightens the look of the series next to its more saturated purple and magenta relatives. Its trailing habit can extend several feet over the course of a season, making it a strong choice for elevated hanging baskets, window boxes, and tall urns where the stems can drape freely. Bloom is continuous from spring through frost with good heat tolerance and minimal deadheading needed. Feed regularly and trim back hard in midsummer if stems become overly long and sparse at the base.

common_name: Mediopicta Alba Century Plant (White-Striped Variegated Agave)

planting.note: Plant pups or container-grown stock in spring in extremely well-drained, sandy to rocky, lean soil in full sun; Mediopicta Alba forms the same massive rosette as the straight species but each thick, gray-green leaf carries a broad, creamy-white central stripe, the reverse pattern from the yellow-margined Marginata cultivar.

directions: Set pups or nursery-grown plants slightly proud of grade in gritty, fast-draining soil in full sun; standing water around the roots causes rapid rot. Mediopicta Alba is one of the showiest variegated century plants, its broad succulent leaves marked with a bold ivory-white band down the center and edged in blue-green, giving each rosette a striking two-tone glow that reads from a distance. Like the species it carries stout marginal teeth and a sharp terminal spine, so it is best sited away from paths and play areas. It is monocarpic, eventually sending up a towering flower stalk after many years of growth and dying back afterward, but it reliably produces basal offsets that can be separated and replanted to continue the display.

common_name: Giant Agave (Pulque Agave, Maguey)

planting.note: Plant offsets or container-grown specimens in spring in extremely well-drained, sandy to rocky, lean soil in full sun; give this species plenty of room, since it forms one of the largest rosettes of any commonly cultivated agave.

directions: Plant in full sun in lean, extremely well-drained soil, allowing generous room to spread; giant agave forms an enormous, dense rosette of thick, gray-green to blue-gray leaves armed with a stout terminal spine and hooked marginal teeth, making it one of the boldest architectural specimens available for large-scale dry landscapes. It is the classic source of pulque and is also used in some mezcal production in central Mexico, where the sugary sap of the mature plant is fermented. After 10-20+ years of slow growth the rosette sends up a massive branched flower stalk that can reach 15-25 feet, then the parent rosette dies, leaving behind offsets that continue the clump. Site it well away from foot traffic given its size and sharp spines.

common_name: Mountain Agave (Hardy Mexican Mountain Agave)

planting.note: Plant offsets or container-grown stock in very well-drained, rocky to gritty, dry soil in full sun; mountain agave is native to high-elevation cloud forest and pine-oak woodland in Nuevo Leon, Mexico, and is among the most cold-tolerant agaves available, surviving temperatures well below 0F when drainage is sharp.

directions: Plant offsets or nursery stock in very well-drained, rocky or gritty soil in full sun; mountain agave forms a broad, symmetrical rosette of wide, dark green to gray-green leaves with reddish-brown terminal spines and distinctive imprinted bud patterning etched into each leaf face from the tightly folded emerging growth. Collected from high-elevation sites in the Sierra Madre Oriental, it tolerates far colder winters than most agaves, making it a favorite of gardeners in the mountain West and other regions too cold for typical agave species. After many years the mature rosette produces a tall flower spike and then dies, leaving offsets behind. An outstanding, boldly architectural accent for rock gardens and dry slopes in colder xeriscape climates.

common_name: Jaws Agave (Toothy-Margined Hardy Agave)

planting.note: Plant offsets in very well-drained, rocky to gritty, dry soil in full sun; Jaws is a selected form of the cold-hardy Agave gentryi from the Sierra Madre Oriental, prized for its dramatically toothed leaf margins.

directions: Plant offsets in very well-drained, gritty or rocky soil in full sun; Jaws forms a tight, symmetrical rosette of broad, blue-green leaves whose margins are lined with large, closely spaced, hooked teeth that resemble a row of shark's teeth, giving the cultivar its name and making it one of the most dramatic-looking hardy agaves. It shares the cold tolerance of the species, handling winter lows into the low teens Fahrenheit with sharp drainage, which makes it a reliable choice well beyond the range of tender tropical agaves. Like other true agaves it is monocarpic, eventually flowering once after many years of growth and then dying back while offsets carry on the clump. An excellent bold specimen for rock gardens and dry, sunny borders.

common_name: Cream Spike Agave (Variegated Applanata Agave)

planting.note: Plant offsets or container-grown stock in spring in extremely well-drained, gritty soil in full sun to light shade; Cream Spike is a variegated selection of Agave applanata grown for its broad, cream-yellow leaf margins around a glaucous blue-gray center.

directions: Plant offsets in extremely well-drained, lean, gritty soil in full sun to light afternoon shade in the hottest climates; Cream Spike forms a dense, compact rosette of broad, flattened, glaucous blue-gray leaves edged in a bright cream-yellow band, with dark, prominent terminal spines that leave decorative imprint patterns on the developing leaves. Its refined size and strong color contrast make it an excellent choice for containers, raised beds, and small-space xeriscape accents where larger agaves would overwhelm the design. It is somewhat less cold-hardy than desert species, so provide winter protection or reflected heat at the cooler edge of its range. Remove offsets to propagate and to keep the clump tidy.

common_name: Texas Yellow Buckeye (Yellow-Flowered Red Buckeye)

planting.note: Plant container-grown or bare-root stock in late winter to early spring in rocky, well-drained, neutral to alkaline soil in partial shade to full sun; this Edwards Plateau limestone native tolerates drier, thinner soils than typical red buckeye.

directions: Plant in rocky, well-drained, neutral to alkaline soil in partial shade to full sun; this naturally occurring yellow-flowered variety of red buckeye is found wild only on the limestone slopes and canyons of the western Edwards Plateau in central Texas, where it grows smaller and more shrubby than the typical red-flowered species, usually 5 to 15 feet tall. In spring it bears upright 6-10 inch panicles of pale to vivid yellow tubular flowers that draw hummingbirds and native bees, and where its range overlaps with the red-flowered form, orange and bicolor hybrids appear. Like other red buckeyes it drops its leaves by mid-to-late summer in response to heat and drought, a normal dormancy rather than a sign of decline, and all plant parts including the seeds are toxic if ingested.
sources: Lady Bird Johnson Wildflower Center — Aesculus pavia var. flavescens plant profile
Texas A&M AgriLife Extension — Plants of Texas Rangelands

common_name: Grey's Littleleaf Yaupon Holly (Fine-Textured Native Holly)

planting.note: Plant container shrubs in late winter, spring, or fall in well-drained soil in full sun to partial shade; prune in late winter once hard freezes have passed to preserve the fine, dense texture.

directions: Plant in well-drained, average soil in full sun to partial shade; like other yaupon selections it shrugs off heat, drought, wind, salt spray, and poor soil once established. Grey's Littleleaf is a dense, multi-stemmed, mounding form distinguished by tiny, glossy, oval leaves that emerge brick-red in spring and hold dark green through winter, giving the shrub an unusually fine, delicate texture rare among broadleaf evergreens. It matures into a rounded 8-to-10-foot mass useful as a specimen accent, informal screen, or large container thriller, and needs only occasional shaping rather than the regular shearing that smaller dwarf yaupon selections often receive.

common_name: Majestic Beauty Southern Magnolia

planting.note: Plant container or balled-and-burlapped trees in late winter, spring, or fall in moist, well-drained, slightly acidic soil in full sun; give it room to develop its broad pyramidal crown.

directions: Plant in moist, fertile, well-drained soil in full sun; avoid low, poorly drained sites where Southern magnolia dislikes wet feet. Majestic Beauty is a vigorous, large-growing selection prized for its extra-large, glossy dark green leaves with dense rusty-brown felted undersides and its unusually heavy, profuse bloom of huge, fragrant, cup-shaped white flowers through summer. Lower branches typically sweep down to the ground, forming a dense, broad pyramidal crown that works well as a single specimen, large screen, or windbreak on properties with room for its mature spread. Established trees are tough and low-maintenance, needing supplemental water mainly during establishment and extended drought.

common_name: Symmes Select Southern Magnolia

planting.note: Plant container or balled-and-burlapped trees in late winter, spring, or fall in moist, well-drained, slightly acidic soil in full sun to partial shade.

directions: Plant in moist, fertile, well-drained soil in full sun to partial shade; Southern magnolia dislikes standing water. Symmes Select was chosen from a seedling growing in an Atlanta cemetery and is valued for its full, dense, well-branched habit and unusually large flowers produced even on young trees, well ahead of the decade-plus wait typical of seed-grown Southern magnolias. Its robust, compact-for-the-species growth and heavy bloom make it a strong choice where a classic, tidy pyramidal form is wanted for a specimen tree or screen. Tolerant of heat, humidity, wind, and coastal conditions once established.

common_name: Baby Grand Magnolia (Dwarf Southern Magnolia)

planting.note: Plant container shrubs in late winter, spring, or fall in moist, well-drained, slightly acidic soil in full sun to partial shade; suits foundation beds and smaller lots that cannot accommodate a full-size Southern magnolia.

directions: Plant in moist, fertile, well-drained soil in full sun to partial shade. Baby Grand is a true dwarf Southern magnolia selection, maturing into a dense, rounded, mounding shrub only about 8 to 10 feet tall and wide, far smaller than even compact cultivars like Little Gem. Broad, glossy dark green leaves with fuzzy rust-brown undersides set off large, creamy white, lemon-scented flowers borne over a long spring-to-summer season. Its compact size makes it a practical choice for foundation plantings, mixed borders, and smaller residential landscapes where a full-size magnolia would be unmanageable, and it needs only routine watering during establishment.
